summary: Specifies the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol, which carries PPP sessions through an IP network. It is a standards-track protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) carries PPP frames through a packet network between an access concentrator and a network server. Its control messages create and manage the tunnel, while data messages carry the PPP traffic.

how does l2tp set up a tunnel
what is the difference between a lac and lns
subtitle: L2TP tunnels PPP sessions from an access concentrator to a network server.

tldr.problem: A PPP session normally ends at the device that accepts the user's link, even when the network service is provided elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: A L2TP Access Concentrator tunnels PPP frames to an L2TP Network Server. A reliable control connection sets up tunnels and sessions, while a separate data channel carries the frames.
tldr.outcome: The PPP session can end at a different device from the access link, and multiple sessions can share a tunnel. RFC 2661 has been updated by RFC 9601.

today: RFC 2661 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999. It has been updated by RFC 9601, so read the documents together.

sections.title: Separating the Access Link from PPP
sections.content:
Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) carries network traffic over a point-to-point link. In a conventional remote-access setup, the link ends at a Network Access Server (NAS), and the PPP session also ends there.

L2TP separates those endpoints. A nearby access concentrator receives the user's link and tunnels the PPP frames across a packet network to the server where the PPP session ends. The RFC also describes using this arrangement to bring separate channels of a multilink PPP bundle to one server.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TP lets the device receiving a user's connection differ from the device running the PPP session. It carries the PPP frames between those devices through a packet network.

sections.title: Roles, Tunnels and Sessions
sections.content:
The L2TP Access Concentrator (LAC) forwards packets between the remote system and its peer. The L2TP Network Server (LNS) is the logical endpoint of the tunneled PPP session. A host running L2TP can act as a client without a separate LAC.

A tunnel connects a LAC and LNS and contains one control connection plus zero or more sessions. Each established session corresponds to one call and carries one PPP stream. Multiple sessions can share a tunnel, and the peers can have multiple tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: The LAC receives the user's link; the LNS ends the PPP session. The tunnel between them can carry several sessions, with one PPP stream in each session.

sections.title: The L2TP Message Header
sections.content:
Control and data messages share a header. Its type bit distinguishes control messages from data messages, while tunnel and session identifiers direct each message to the intended recipient. Each endpoint chooses its own identifiers, so a message carries the identifier assigned by the receiving peer.

Control messages always include the length and sequence fields. The version field must be 2, and packets with an unknown version must be discarded. Optional fields can include the message length, sequence numbers and an offset that marks where the payload begins.
sections.plainLanguage: The header tells the receiver whether a message manages the tunnel or carries PPP data. It also identifies the receiving tunnel and session.

sections.title: Control Messages and Attribute Pairs
sections.content:
Control messages contain Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs). Each AVP identifies a vendor and attribute type, then carries its value; the length field is at most 1023 octets.

The Mandatory bit determines whether a receiver can ignore an unknown AVP. If that bit is set, an unknown AVP ends the related session or tunnel; otherwise, the receiver ignores it. The Hidden bit can obscure sensitive values when the peers share a secret, using a random vector and an MD5-based procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages are made from labeled fields that describe the requested operation. A required field the receiver does not understand ends the relevant session or tunnel.

sections.title: Opening Tunnels and Sessions
sections.content:
The peers first establish a control connection with SCCRQ, SCCRP and SCCCN messages. This exchange identifies the peers and communicates protocol, framing and bearer capabilities. Tunnel authentication is optional; if a peer issues a challenge, the other side must provide the matching response or the tunnel is not established.

After the tunnel is ready, the peers establish a session for each call. For an incoming call, the LAC sends ICRQ, the LNS answers with ICRP, and the LAC completes setup with ICCN. Either peer can end a session with CDN or close the tunnel and its sessions with StopCCN.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers establish the tunnel before opening any sessions. They then exchange call messages to create a session, and either peer can later close a session or the whole tunnel.

sections.title: Data Delivery and Control Reliability
sections.content:
The LAC removes link framing and CRC information, encapsulates each PPP frame in an L2TP data message, and sends it through the tunnel. Data messages are not retransmitted. Optional data sequence numbers can help detect loss or restore ordering, but do not make delivery reliable.

Control messages use sequence numbers and a sliding window for reliable, ordered delivery. A message without acknowledgement is retransmitted with exponential backoff. Hello messages help distinguish a failed tunnel from one that is simply idle. Over IP, L2TP uses UDP port 1701 by default.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP data travels without L2TP retransmission, though sequence numbers can reveal loss or reordering. Control messages are numbered, acknowledged and retransmitted when needed.

sections.title: Authentication and Packet Protection
sections.content:
The optional tunnel challenge authenticates the peer during setup, but does not protect later packets from snooping or injection. L2TP relies on its underlying transport for confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. For IP transport, the RFC describes using IPsec to protect L2TP packets between the LAC and LNS.

Proxy PPP authentication trusts the LAC to report authentication information correctly. An LNS that supports this feature must be able to disable it and require a new PPP authentication exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup challenge does not encrypt or authenticate every later packet. The RFC describes IPsec as a way to protect L2TP traffic between the tunnel endpoints.
